Renee of France
re-nā' of frans
n. (Renee de France, 1510–1574, duchess of Ferrara, protector of the Reformed)
Latin renata, born again, through French Renee; a royal daughter of France.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Renee of France was a daughter of Louis XII, married to the duke of Ferrara, and for twenty years she kept a court in Italy where Reformed convictions could be held and Reformed fugitives could be sheltered. Calvin visited her in 1536 and corresponded with her for the rest of her life, and his letters to her are among the most searching he ever wrote, because she wavered. Under pressure from her husband, the Inquisition and her own son she conformed outwardly more than once, and Calvin told her so plainly. When widowed she returned to France, settled at Montargis, and turned the chateau into a refuge during the wars of religion, protecting hundreds. The dictionary gives her the Chronicler's kind of verdict: a mixed record, ending better than it ran, and a house that became the Shunammite's chamber on a princely scale (2Ki 4:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines protection as defence and shelter from evil, and dissemble as to hide under a false appearance.

expand to see more

PROTEC'TION, n. Defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss, injury or annoyance.

DISSEM'BLE, v.t. To hide under a false appearance; to conceal the real fact, motives, intention or sentiments.

DUCH'ESS, n. The consort or widow of a duke; also, a lady who has the sovereignty of a dukedom.

WA'VER, v.i. To fluctuate; to be unsettled in opinion; to vacillate; to be undetermined.

Key Scripture

2Ki 4:10 — "Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither."

Heb 13:2 — "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

1Th 5:21 — "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

Psa 90:17 — "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."

Modern Corruption

A French princess in Ferrara who wavered, and a chateau that sheltered hundreds.

expand to see more

The record is given whole. Renee of France protected the persecuted at real risk, and she also dissembled when the pressure came, attending the mass she had been taught to regard as idolatry in order to keep her position and her children. Calvin wrote to her about it without flattery, as he wrote to other great persons, and the dictionary follows him rather than the modern habit of treating a patron's usefulness as settling the question of her faithfulness.

The principle to recover is that protection of the persecuted is a real and commended work, and that it does not purchase exemption from the command to prove all things and hold fast what is good. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). The shelter itself is counted: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2). And the prayer for a mixed life's work is the psalmist's: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).

Usage

"“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) — Calvin's letters, written without flattery."

"“Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2) — Montargis in the wars of religion."

"“establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17) — a mixed record, ending better."
